items.title: Heroes Save Lives During In-N-Out Burger Shooting and Company Owner Unveils Powerful ‘God’ Message
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Pray.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Lynsi Snyder, owner and president of In-N-Out Burger, offered a prayer and public response over the weekend to a tragic shooting at one of her company’s Idaho restaurant locations that left three dead and at least seven people injured.

Listen to the latest episode of “Quick Start”

Snyder said one of the three killed at the location in Twin Falls, Idaho, was a restaurant worker. The tragic event reportedly unfolded Aug. 1, when suspect Chad Williams, 24, allegedly attacked the site and then took his own life, according to authorities.

One witness claimed the shooter randomly fired at people in their vehicles and through the drive-thru window.

“My heart is broken, my chest is heavy, my eyes burn from the tears I’ve shed,” Snyder wrote in a press release. “We lost one of our beautiful Associates tonight. She was taking care of our most important asset — our Customers, and her life was taken by a disgusting human who doesn’t value the lives of others or his own.”

Snyder continued, “He shot both on our property and off, and ended his life shortly after he took the precious lives of our Associate and Customers, innocent people who never saw it coming.”

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Lynsi Snyder (@lynsi_snyder)

The owner of the popular fast-food chain went on to say that the company will mourn with the families and pray for them as they navigate this difficult season.

“I am no stranger to loss, but this is so incredibly tough, and my heart also goes out to all of the Associates and Customers who were there during this traumatic event,” Synder said. “I love you all, and I ask you to turn to God, not in anger, but seeking comfort and strength for those who are hurting.”

Twin Falls police said two heroes — an off-duty state trooper and an armed citizen — intervened and saved lives. The two reportedly fired at the man and were able to distract the attacker enough to save lives, USA Today reported.

“We believe their actions helped drive the suspect away from the scene, preventing further casualties,” Twin Falls police Chief Matthew Hicks said, going on to commend the citizen and officer for their “heroic action to stop this incident.”

Two of the people injured during the incident still remain in critical condition. Continue to pray for the victims and families impacted by this horrific tragedy.

items.title: The China Strategy Hollywood Doesn’t Want You to Know About
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Important.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

A Hollywood producer who spent years courting China to support American film studios is now speaking out against Tinseltown’s attempts to work with the communist nation.

Christopher Fenton, producer of the new film, “Bad Counselors,” told CBN News Hollywood is always trying to find new businesses and new sources of capital to help make expensive films and projects possible.

“Then, on top of it, on the output side of things … once you actually get it into theaters, are there markets there that we haven’t explored?” he said, detailing the questions executives are often faced with. “Are there potential ways to generate new revenue?”

Decades ago, he said the U.S. approach to China started to shift, with America opening up more relations with the nation. While America initially had a “frozen relationship” with China, an idea took root: that the more products and services the U.S. could get into the nation, the “more we would spread the aspirational quality of democracy inside of a communist country.”

In addition to growing the economy in the U.S., Fenton said there was a higher mission and purpose in engaging China and opening up the market.

“What we found over time … is that aspirational quality of democracy inside a communist country plan hasn’t really worked out all that well,” he said.

Fenton said jobs were generated and GDP growth came, but that it was only a “sugar high” that didn’t last. Overall, he said Hollywood’s market share in China has been lost. The initial plans simply didn’t pan out the way he and others wanted.

“The initial thought was the more products and services we could get in that country, the better, no matter what it took to get them in,” he said. “So it was like an ends-justify-the-means plan.”

While 99% of people seeking to engage China in this way were looking to help the U.S., he said the other “1% was very willing to sell out the soul of America to make a buck.”

Regardless of the mission, there was an unintended consequence of the relationship between China and the U.S. — and it involved bias and a quest for the communist party to push its ideologies on the masses.

“For the most part, we were under this other higher mission,” he said. “And part of that for Beijing and the entertainment content space was to placate them and their directives in terms of messaging and narrative, the way they wanted their system of government presented to their own people to essentially make that 1.3 billion people just happy enough that they don’t revolt and have another Tiananmen Square incident like June 4, 1989.”

But it didn’t end there.

“Essentially they saw it as a propaganda engine in the West, this Hollywood content ecosystem,” Fenton said. “To essentially take and trumpet their messaging and narratives around the world.”

He cited the film “Looper,” which he produced, as an example. Fenton said the time-travel film initially depicted a future utopian society in France.

“But Beijing said, ‘If you want access to our market, you need to change your time travel story to one where China is the utopian place to live, where the weight of the world is shifting, and if you change the plot to be where everybody wants to be someday is China, we’ll let you have that movie in,'” Fenton said. “So we actually completely changed the script, completely changed the narrative to be pro-Beijing, pro-China in order to get access to that market.”

He continued, “It gave us a top 10 movie that year in the market, and no one else in the world noticed the fact that they were digesting propaganda from what was a pretty good movie.”

Fenton said this sort of dynamic might not be as prevalent right now as “the golden goose of China is sort of cooked right now,” with many people and businesses moving away from the communist country.

“This kind of propaganda, this kind of messaging, this kind of control over narrative globally is across all industries,” he said. “So yes, entertainment business is sort of the easiest one to see because we tell stories that prepare that narrative and messaging from Beijing, but it’s happening in all industries in the way they’re throttled on certain things they can say or the things that they really might not want to say or things that they need to trumpet are amplified and they’re pushed to amplify.”

Listen to the latest episode of “Quick Start”

He said these portrayals affect how young Americans view China, with some believing there are incredible buildings, skyscrapers, and happy people everywhere.

“They see nothing bad about China,” he said. “And it’s why we’re starting to see Pew studies show that people actually think more favorably in terms of China than they do the United States.”

This framing is one reason why Fenton is now pushing for films and projects to be made in America. His new film, “Bad Counselors,” is an example of a movie that was fully created here in the US.

“We wanted all American backdrops,” he said. “We shot in North Carolina. We did a little in Texas, a little in Tennessee. We used all vendors that were American and we fully employed Americans, your brethren, my brethren. We made sure that we took care of our citizens.”

The premise of “Bad Counselors” is comical — and very American.

“Two frat bros must become church bros, fast,” the synopsis reads. “After one wild night ends in handcuffs and a campus police escort, two best friends are slapped with 120 hours of community service due in two weeks, or they’re expelled. Their genius plan? Pose as counselors at a local Christian youth camp, where every sing-along, campfire devotional, and trust fall counts toward the clock. Just one problem (okay, three): they don’t like kids, they hate camping, and they have barely set foot in a church.”

items.title: Family in God
items.author: Arthur Jackson
items.summary: “What makes you smile when you think about your son?” That was my question for Clarence—a younger man I was mentoring. The proud father proceeded to share some of his bright four-year-old’s accomplishments. One particular response left me amused. Not only does the child have
items.content:
📖 Devotional | Our Daily Bread

“What makes you smile when you think about your son?” That was my question for Clarence—a younger man I was mentoring. The proud father proceeded to share some of his bright four-year-old’s accomplishments. One particular response left me amused. Not only does the child have his father’s first and last names, but he already looks so much like his father that he can unlock his father’s smart phone using the facial recognition feature!

In John 14, Jesus made it clear how closely He resembled His Father. When an inquisitive Philip requested, “Lord, show us the Father” (v. 8), Jesus responded, “Don’t you know me, Philip, even after I have been among you such a long time? Anyone who has seen me has seen the Father” (v. 9). How was it that the Father was revealed through the Son? It was through Jesus’ “words” (v. 10) and “works” (v. 11) that God’s love, mercy, grace, and more were brilliantly displayed.  

Empowered by God’s Spirit, believers in Jesus are privileged to share family likeness. The invisible God becomes visible through His children. Regarding Christ-like love, John reminds us, “No one has ever seen God. But if we love each other, God lives in us, and his love is brought to full expression in us” (1 John 4:12 nlt).

What is it about your words and deeds that remind others of Jesus?

items.title: The Help God Provides
items.author: James Banks
items.summary: When commercial fisherman Scott Thompson fell out of his boat one moonless night in the Santa Barbara Channel off the California coast, he didn’t know if he’d survive. He swam hard after the boat, but the motor was running and he couldn’t reach it. So he attempted swimming to a dis
items.content:
📖 Devotional | Our Daily Bread

When commercial fisherman Scott Thompson fell out of his boat one moonless night in the Santa Barbara Channel off the California coast, he didn’t know if he’d survive. He swam hard after the boat, but the motor was running and he couldn’t reach it. So he attempted swimming to a distant oil platform in the darkness. Beginning to lose hope, Thompson heard a splash in the cold water near him. A harbor seal swam with him for a while, nudging him along toward the platform. Five hours later, Thompson completed the long swim and described the seal as “an angel” sent to help him.

The writer of the book of Hebrews describes angels as “ministering spirits sent to serve those who will inherit salvation” (Hebrews 1:14). The passage highlights the greatness of Jesus and emphasizes that angels—wonderful and glorious beings that they are—exist to further His purposes in saving us. Jesus sustains “all things by his powerful word” (v. 3).

All around us is an unseen reality in which God sends angels to aid those who have gladly received the good news of Jesus. Sometimes our nights may be long, and we may wonder if we can keep going. But He’ll always give us the help we need—help that will nudge us on in Him.

items.title: Hosanna Wong: There’s a Difference Between Knowing Who God Says You Are and Living Like It
items.author: Emily Brown
items.summary: For years, Hosanna Wong preached about identity. She traveled the country performing spoken word poetry in prisons, recovery ministries and churches, telling others who they were in God while quietly watering down who she was. Had you found her ministry a decade ago, you wouldn’t have found it
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

For years, Hosanna Wong preached about identity. She traveled the country performing spoken word poetry in prisons, recovery ministries and churches, telling others who they were in God while quietly watering down who she was.

Had you found her ministry a decade ago, you wouldn’t have found it under her name. “Had people known my spoken word ministry 12 years ago, they wouldn’t have known me as Hosanna Wong,” she says. “They would have known me as Hosanna Poetry.”

She had been advised early on that her heritage — her last name, her background — might stand in the way of the ministry she felt called to. She believed it. She went by a pen name for years, trimmed her story to fit the rooms she was in and shaped herself around what she assumed people wanted.

“I found myself constantly trying to fit the mold of whatever group I was with in fear that I could not fully be accepted in these environments,” she says. “So I would water down parts of my story and parts of my background and parts of my real questions.”

That tension between who she was and who she was trying to be is at the center of her new book. “You Are More Than You’ve Been Told,” releasing this August, is Wong’s attempt to give readers what she spent years looking for — not just an understanding of who they are in God, but a practical framework for actually living that way.

“I wanted to tell them who they are, but I also wanted to tell them how,” she says. “Not just who you are, but how do I know who I am every single day? And how do I live as who I really am?”

It’s a question a lot of people in their 20s and 30s are sitting with, often for the first time. And Wong says the struggle is older than any of us.

“The enemy of our souls has been trying to convince us that we are less than we are,” she says. “So we live lives that are less than the lives we’ve been created to live. So you’re not crazy.”

The lies, she says, rarely announce themselves. They come from childhood, from a cruel comment that stuck, from a leader who meant well but got it wrong. Sometimes they come wrapped in a half-truth, which makes them harder to shake. Wong knows this from experience. Her own early wounds came from people who, by her own account, genuinely wanted to see her succeed.

“I think that we believe the lie that we are not enough and our background is not enough and our story is not enough,” she says. “And it has taken me years to understand and see the truth.”

The breakthrough, when it came, was agricultural.

Wong grew up on the streets of San Francisco, the daughter of a former heroin addict and gang member who became a pastor after encountering Jesus. Her father died when she was 18, and she set out on her own, eventually spending four and a half years traveling the country without a home base, living out of guest rooms and spare bedrooms — learning, she says, that the Church could be something different from what had hurt her.

In a season when she felt disconnected — from herself and from God — she called a friend who had spent years working in vineyards in New Zealand and up and down the West Coast. She wanted to understand John 15, where Jesus tells his followers, “I am the vine, you are the branches.” Her friend, who had no knowledge of the scripture, gave her a purely agricultural answer.

All a branch needs to survive is to be connected to the vine, the friend told her. But without a trellis — a structure — “they will live constantly weighed down. They will carry weights they weren’t meant to carry, and they will fight an uphill battle they don’t have to fight.”

Wong says the words stopped her. “I just thought, man, I am feeling weighed down today.”

She came to see the trellis as a metaphor for the rhythms and routines that keep us connected — not just knowing who we are in God, but structuring our lives in a way that keeps that connection alive. The structure, she’s careful to say, is not the source.

“There’s no salvation in the structure,” she says. “There’s only salvation and life in the source.”

But without it, she found, the branches eventually lose their footing — and their connection to the vine.

That realization sent her back to the life of Jesus. She began studying his private rhythms — how he sought solitude, how he engaged with scripture, how his public ministry grew out of what he did when no one was watching — and asking what it would look like to arrange her own life around the same kinds of practices.

“I realized that to reclaim my life and reclaim my identity, I needed to reclaim my schedule,” she says.

One of those practices was engaging with scripture differently — not as a ritual she had grown numb to, but in a way that felt alive. A new translation. A different time of day. Reading with other people and hearing their perspectives. The goal was simple: make God’s voice the loudest voice in her life.

“When people say things to us — you’re not good enough, you’re worthless, you’ll always be defined by your past — it doesn’t match up with what I know is true,” she says, “because I know what God says about me.”

She returned to spoken word poetry after six years away from it. She recorded a piece called “I Have a New Name” — and released it under Hosanna Wong.

“The enemy’s been lying to you because he doesn’t want you to know how important your life is and how powerful your choices are,” she says, “and what it would mean for you to be who you are and share your real story with the people around you.”

The question Wong leaves people with is the same one she had to face herself: not just whether you know who God says you are — but whether you’ve built a life that lets you actually live like it.

items.title: The Church of Wellness Is Not Making the Cut
items.author: Johanna Duncan
items.summary:
Johanna Duncan

It’s much easier to sell stillness than surrender, and much easier to sell a god who asks nothing of you than the one who tends to ask for everything.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Johanna Duncan

A few weeks ago I was invited to a ceramics class. The invitation came with very intentional wording: a chance to slow down, to focus on myself, to immerse myself in the object I create with my hands. I pictured wet clay, a wheel, and I was hoping to create a cute coffee mug I could enjoy every morning. I said yes immediately.

It took about twenty minutes at the ceramics studio for me to realize this wasn’t just a ceramics class. I’d been invited to a pitch meeting for a wellness center. And twenty minutes after that, I realized it wasn’t just a wellness center, it was a place for spiritual awakening.

During the introduction, the owner explained that she saw each of us as spiritually awakened women and that the ceramics were never really about just ceramics; they were a spiritual practice intended to bring us in contact with Mother Nature. The expansion she was raising money for made room for a tarot reading room and a yoga studio, both offered for an extra fee. Once one-on-one, she mentioned she knew I hiked, did Pilates, was crafty, and prayed, all gathered from my Instagram, so naturally she assumed I’d be drawn to a studio that also did tarot and yoga. 

I want to be clear that I don’t think this woman is particularly evil or a con artist. I think she believes every word of it and has the best intentions around it. As I got to work on my coffee mug, I looked around and wondered if anyone else was as uncomfortable as I was. Some people seemed excited about this business venture and shared about similar business concepts they’d seen pop up around the city. I did some research after the event and realized this was bigger than I’d initially thought. Everything this woman presented is part of a worldview and a new form of religion. It’s the near-total merger of wellness and spirituality into a single, undifferentiated category in which pottery, tarot, Pilates, and yoga are all under the same umbrella of spiritual awakening. And it’s intentionally vague, so that it leaves room for the narcissistic project of building your own religion designed on your own terms.

Wellness culture’s attempt to double as religion is not a new invention. It has a well-established philosophical and even commercial lineage: The New Thought and Christian Science “mind-cure” movements of the late 1800s were the first to encourage Americans to dive into the concept that physical health flowed from one’s mental and spiritual state. This suddenly turns health into the center of everything. Then came the human potential movement that grew out of places like Esalen in the 1960s and the New Age boom of the 1980s that first packaged crystals and things like yoga studios for a mass audience, which continues to have commercial success to this day. Each wave promised the same thing: a spirituality without the inconvenience of a Church, assembled from whatever felt useful during your particular season. 

Do this for a few decades and you suddenly end up with what sociologist Robert Bellah described in his 1985 book Habits of the Heart as “Sheilaism.” For this book, he interviewed a young nurse called Sheila, who said that her faith was “just my own little voice,” a personal blend of believing in God, being gentle with herself, and taking care of others with no creed, no congregation, and no one to answer to but herself. Bellah’s point wasn’t that she was uniquely lost. It was that Sheilaism, taken to its logical end, produces the possibility of billions of religions, one for each of us, which is another way of saying no religion at all since a religion that answers only to the person who invented it isn’t binding anyone to anything. 

The wellness industry is Sheilaism with a business plan and a candle budget, and it hasn’t solved the underlying problem any better than Sheila did. If anything, the data on this kind of homemade spirituality is worse than you’d expect. A 2013 study in The British Journal of Psychiatry drawing on roughly 7,400 people in England found that those who describe themselves as spiritual but not religious have significantly higher rates of anxiety, phobias, and other neurotic disorders than either the religious or the plainly nonreligious. A later 2018 study in The Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease fittingly titled “A Lonely Search?” found the same group at greater risk for depression. This isn’t a diagnosis for everyone practicing Sheilaism, but it should put to rest the idea that a self-designed spirituality is equal to religion without the drawbacks. It isn’t. It’s a lonelier version of the same hunger, minus the structure that historically made the hunger both bearable and fruitful.

It isn’t true that everything spiritual is the same. Sitting in silence before God and sitting in silence before yourself are not two dialects of the same language. One asks you to be still so something outside you, something with its own claim on your life, can reach in. It involves some wrestling and sacrifice, and most of its gifts are fruits of these struggles. Meanwhile, the other asks you to be still so you can hear more clearly the sound of your own voice, and it’s shaped by our own self-soothing. That’s the least harmful version of it. There’s another that asks whatever is out there to fill you in, and that is quite dangerous at a spiritual, physical, and emotional level. 
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

Wellness culture is built almost entirely on the second and third posture. It uses the vocabulary of the first, and it engages in the ritual and the sense of the sacred, but it empties it of the one thing that makes it work: the disposition toward encountering God and being changed by the surrender we experience in his presence. That submission is a stark contrast with the temptation of control that comes with seeking to know the future. And it’s not the same to seek to be the best version of ourselves for the sake of sainthood than for vain reasons. 

Connecting with yourself is a real thing, and it can be a genuinely good time. There is nothing wrong with a pottery class that helps you unclench and disconnect for an hour. But in service of what? That’s the question wellness culture rarely asks and even more rarely responds to because the answer is often in service of yourself. That in itself isn’t always a bad thing, because we do have a responsibility to take care of ourselves, but as a form of religion, it never suffices.

And when “more you” is the entire goal with no outside reference point, no tradition, no moral demand, no God to submit oneself to, the practice stops pointing anywhere. It eventually loses value. What was supposed to be self-connection curdles into something closer to self-management and eventually into something closer to control. Because no matter how good your life is and how many blessings surround you, there’s always something to be a god of, always something stubbornly out of your hands. Suddenly there’s no room for surprises or for God’s will, and that does come with a cost. What started as well meaning becomes a very well-decorated form of narcissism, one that is very easy to justify and fall for.

I’ve started to notice a pattern in who this kind of “spirituality” attracts most, and it’s not only the burned-out, the lost, or the genuinely searching. It’s the high achievers. The type A people with real perfectionist streaks who have spent their whole lives optimizing everything else—career, body, calendar—and have now turned those same mechanisms on their inner world. Wellness becomes the next project to master, the next domain to get right, the next area where falling short feels unacceptable. It’s therapy repackaged for people who don’t actually want to be undone by the process, just refined by it. Real transformation asks you to lose control for a while, to grow in humility and let go. But this version lets you keep it and calls it “growth.”

That’s the part that actually unsettled me about that studio, more than the pitch itself. It wasn’t that the owner assumed this was worth my money. It’s that she genuinely couldn’t see the difference between doing Pilates, crafts, or hiking for the sake of pleasure and well-being and doing those things with the expectation of having a spiritual experience. She’d flattened the whole spiritual landscape into one marketable feeling, and she isn’t alone in that. A huge amount of the wellness economy runs on exactly this flattening because seeking one’s well-being has become a matter of seeking false gods. And now you can purchase all of it through a well-marketed and hobby comprehensive membership.

But real spiritual traditions were never built like that. The Church has doctrine, discipline, community, accountability, and, crucially, a claim on your heart that isn’t about you. It demands obedience, not just good intentions or the desire for your own well-being. Prayer isn’t a mood you curate; it’s a conversation with Someone who might ask something of you in return. It’s building a relationship that requires surrender and being changed by God rather than by your own five-year plan. That’s precisely the part wellness culture discards because it’s the part that’s actually uncomfortable. It’s much easier to sell stillness than surrender, and much easier to sell a god who asks nothing of you than the one who tends to ask for everything.

These wellness memberships can and are canceled the moment it stops serving you. It also has no answer for suffering because while wellness can help us cope, it was never built to carry that weight. It treats suffering as something to manage and optimize. It’s all about inflammation to reduce or trauma to process, which is nice until something happens that can’t be juiced or journaled away, and self-compassion can’t forgive you for what you did to someone else, or hold you accountable in your own shame, or reconcile you with God. That wrestling is everything, but the church of wellness softens it into something too comfortable to be worthwhile.

This isn’t just theory, and my experience at the ceramics studio that day is not a fluke. In the last year, two women in exactly this kind of spirituality walked away from it, in public (thank you, Instagram). Shannon Fairweather, a Survivor 49 contestant who ran a New Age wellness community and described herself on national television as “hippie, spiritual, love the energy of the moon,” spent the show praying to the ocean, the moon, and various spirit guides. She’s since announced she’s converting to Catholicism, drawn in by the Eucharist and the Mass, saying, “After years of searching, I can finally say that I am home.” Around the same time, Alex Reads Tarot, a TikTok creator with around a million followers and 58 million likes built entirely on tarot readings, posted a video announcing she was deleting every piece of tarot content she’d ever made because in her words, “Jesus Christ has saved my life, and I can no longer ignore that reality.” She lost roughly thirty thousand followers within days and hasn’t posted since. Neither woman was burned out or chasing a gimmick. Both had already reached the top of the exact economy that the studio owner was trying to recruit me for; and in their honest pursuit for truth, both walked away from it once they came face-to-face with the reality of what it’s like to have an encounter and relationship with Christ. 

Wellness can absolutely be important and a good time. It can lower your heart rate, improve your posture, and give you an hour of quiet you badly needed. What it can’t do, no matter how many candles are lit around it, is stand in for the thing it keeps imitating and trying to replace: Christ’s bride, the Church.

items.title: Tuesday, August 4, 2026
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, in today’s Gospel, Jesus comes to his disciples walking on the water.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Daily Reading


First Reading
Jeremiah 30:1-2, 12-15, 18-22

The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord: Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: Write in a book all the words that I have spoken to you.

For thus says the Lord:
Your hurt is incurable,
    your wound is grievous.
There is no one to uphold your cause,
    no medicine for your wound,
    no healing for you.
All your lovers have forgotten you;
    they care nothing for you;
for I have dealt you the blow of an enemy,
    the punishment of a merciless foe,
because your guilt is great,
    because your sins are so numerous.
Why do you cry out over your hurt?
    Your pain is incurable.
Because your guilt is great,
    because your sins are so numerous,
    I have done these things to you.
Thus says the Lord:
I am going to restore the fortunes of the tents of Jacob,
    and have compassion on his dwellings;
the city shall be rebuilt upon its mound,
    and the citadel set on its rightful site.
Out of them shall come thanksgiving,
    and the sound of merrymakers.
I will make them many, and they shall not be few;
    I will make them honored, and they shall not be disdained.
Their children shall be as of old,
    their congregation shall be established before me;
    and I will punish all who oppress them.
Their prince shall be one of their own,
    their ruler shall come from their midst;
I will bring him near, and he shall approach me,
    for who would otherwise dare to approach me?
says the Lord.
And you shall be my people,
    and I will be your God.

Psalm
Psalm 102:16-18, 19-21, 29, 22-23

For the Lord will build up Zion;
    he will appear in his glory.
He will regard the prayer of the destitute,
    and will not despise their prayer.
Let this be recorded for a generation to come,
    so that a people yet unborn may praise the Lord:
that he looked down from his holy height,
    from heaven the Lord looked at the earth,
to hear the groans of the prisoners,
    to set free those who were doomed to die;
so that the name of the Lord may be declared in Zion,
    and his praise in Jerusalem,
when peoples gather together,
    and kingdoms, to worship the Lord.
He has broken my strength in midcourse;
    he has shortened my days.

Gospel Reading
Matthew 14:22-36

Immediately he made the disciples get into the boat and go on ahead to the other side, while he dismissed the crowds. And after he had dismissed the crowds, he went up the mountain by himself to pray. When evening came, he was there alone, but by this time the boat, battered by the waves, was far from the land, for the wind was against them. And early in the morning he came walking toward them on the sea. But when the disciples saw him walking on the sea, they were terrified, saying, “It is a ghost!” And they cried out in fear. But immediately Jesus spoke to them and said, “Take heart, it is I; do not be afraid.”

Peter answered him, “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the water.” He said, “Come.” So Peter got out of the boat, started walking on the water, and came toward Jesus. But when he noticed the strong wind, he became frightened, and beginning to sink, he cried out, “Lord, save me!” Jesus immediately reached out his hand and caught him, saying to him, “You of little faith, why did you doubt?” When they got into the boat, the wind ceased. And those in the boat worshiped him, saying, “Truly you are the Son of God.”

When they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret. After the people of that place recognized him, they sent word throughout the region and brought all who were sick to him, and begged him that they might touch even the fringe of his cloak; and all who touched it were healed.

Reflection

Friends, in today’s Gospel, Jesus comes to his disciples walking on the water. Whenever we encounter the disciples in a boat, we are dealing with the Church, the barque of Peter. Here we see the beginning of the Church’s journey through time.

Winds and waves toss the barque. Anyone acquainted with Church history knows the truth of this—and it’s a special comfort for those enduring our tumultuous times. We are engaged in a spiritual warfare, a battle not against flesh and blood but against powers and principalities.

Early in the morning, the disciples see Jesus coming toward them, “walking on the sea.” Terrified, they cry out. But Jesus calms them with the words “Take courage, it is I; do not be afraid.” Then Peter says, “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the water.”

Peter stands preeminently for the Church across the ages. And here is the Church at its best, reaching out in confidence to Christ. The fruit of that confidence is participation in the Lord’s power: “Peter got out of the boat and began to walk on the water toward Jesus.” Relying on our own power, we can do nothing. But relying on him, we can do anything.
